subject: hazard rate parameters are highly correlated

messages.author: 25f1a211d8ac38c0
messages.subject: hazard rate parameters are highly correlated
parts:
Distance experts,

=20

I am running analysis on a group of songbirds where the data was
collected using point transects. For one species, specifically northern
bobwhite, I have received a warning with all hazard rate models
indicating the two parameters of the hazard rate key function are highly
correlated. Why would this be and is it something I need to worry

about? =20

=20

Thanks for your help,

=20

messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: hazard rate parameters are highly correlated
parts:
Hi Lindesey, list,

Simple answer: so long as the fit looks sensible and the correlation is
not 1 then it is probably nothing to worry about. Otherwise you may
want to try setting start values or constraining the parameters to help
it produce a sensible fit. If your data are "gnarly" in some way, you
may want to avoid the hazard rate.

Longer answer: Distance fits the detection function models by maximum
likelihood. The hazard rate has two parameters: one governing shape and
one scale (see Fig 2.6 of the Intro book). So, you can think of a 3-d
plot with shape and scale on the x and y axis and likelihood (actually
log likelihood) on the z axis. Distance attempts to find the top of the
hill -- the highest point on the z axis, and then reports the values of
the shape and scale parameter at that point. For some data, the hill
shows a strong ridge along the top, rather than a point. This is an
indication that the parameters are correlated. If the correlation is
perfect (i.e., 1) then only a linear combination of shape and scale are
identifiable, and not each individual parameter separately. Then,
variance on the estimate of f(0) would likely blow up. However, this
rarely (ever?) happens in Distance for the hazard rate model with no
covariates. Distance warns you when the correlation is very high
(>0.999 I think). This is because when correlation is high, it may have
trouble finding the top of the ridge, and hence identifying values for
the parameters. (You can check the estimated correlation on the
Detection Fct/Global/Parameter Estimates page of output at the bottom.)
So, ask yourself if the fitted function it came up with looks sensible
and fits the data well. If not, it may be that Distance failed to find
the maximum, so perhaps manually choosing start values may help, if you
can think of sensible start points; also constraining the parameter
values can help (e.g., constraining the scale parameter between so it
can not get too high). Distance sometimes has trouble fitting hazard
rate functions to very spiked data, when the shape parameter is
estimated to be at, or close to 1 (the lower bound set by default for
this parameter). If you have spiked data, you need to ask the usual
question about why you have this and what kind of a fit you want (I
expect his has been discussed before on the list). If you have a small
dataset and this is happening (I'm not sure why it would, however), you
may want to avoid the hazard rate function completely and stick with 1
parameter models if you think they can adequately represent the true
detection function shape.

Hope this helps. If this doesn't make sense given your data then please
send me your project (zipped up using File | Export) and I'll check it
out. If others have insights on high correlation please feel free to
chip in!

- len
